Kinda old, but some of the best games I've ever played are Zeus: Master of Olympus (has an expansion called Poseidon: Master of Atlantis), Dungeon Keeper 2, and Dwarf Fortress.

Zeus: Master of Olympus is almost completely economy based. It's a simpler version of Anno that requires less expansion gameplay and instead relies on setting up a single city to be perfect. You don't have the massive amount of space that Anno usually provides; organizing your city is half the battle, especially in the Atlantis expansion.

Dungeon Keeper 2 has you play as the bad guy. You own a dungeon. You recruit monsters. You order your slaves to build areas that monsters like and put your monsters to work, either as mechanics to build traps, researchers to add to your underworld's knowledge, or train them to be defenders against the waves of holy warriors trying to loot your kingdom. It has a lot of combat, but has a heavy focus on defensive gameplay, making it one of my favorite RTS games ever.

Dwarf Fortress is like the Sims mixed with Minecraft, with the difficulty knob turned up so hard that it got broken off. It's kinda complicated to learn, but no other game has the complexity of Dwarf Fortress. The game is extremely old and gets massive updates every year or so. Look up the "Lazy Newb Pack", which gives you several necessities to make your life much easier, including replacement graphics (the original game looks like ASCII symbols) and the Dwarf Therapist program (makes managing your dwarves much easier, almost a necessity).

On a side note, Zeus has you organize your city into "sectors" that you separate using dividers. Instead of having an AI figure out where to go, each service runs in a loop, and doesn't ever pass dividers. Think of it like having an ice-cream truck that circles the same block until it runs out of icecream, which then it'll go back home to restock. If you want another block to be stocked with icecream, prepare to build another truck.

DK2 has little economy and more strategy. Build your library in someplace quiet. Build your training grounds near the exit to your dungeon so that if you get invaded, your fighters are already packed in one place. There's only one currency, and it can run out fairly easily if you get lax on the job.

DF is extremely complicated to start out. Items usually can't be used if they aren't in a stockpile. So if you want a farm, you need a stockpile to hold the seeds, so the farm can take them, then a stockpile to hold the food the farm makes, then you need a brewery to take the fruit and turn it into beer, but to do that you need barrels, but to make barrels you need a carpenter's workshop, but to use a carpenter's workshop you need wood, and to use the wood you need a wood stockpile, and to harvest the wood you need an axe and a few trees that you have designated to chop down, and after all that they still need a dining area where they'll feel comfortable drinking in.

And that's just what you need to make sure your dwarves don't die of thirst. They don't drink water, they only drink alcohol. Don't let any of this discourage you, though. Building a city from the ground up takes a lot of work, but also gives you the greatest sense of accomplishment any game could give. Until a necromancer army comes and wrecks your day. There's no winning Dwarf Fortress, only glorious or unfortunate deaths.
